arrest:
- In India, police can sometimes arrest a person without a warrant, but whether they may do so depends on the nature of the alleged offence and the circumstances at the time.  
- Generally, for serious offences (often called cognizable offences) the police are empowered to make an arrest without first obtaining a warrant.  
- For less serious offences (non‑cognizable offences), a warrant is usually required unless a magistrate has already given permission.  
- Even when a warrant‑less arrest is allowed, the police must have reasonable grounds to believe that the person has committed the offence and must follow the procedural safeguards that apply.  
- If you are arrested, you have the right to be told the reason for the arrest, to inform a family member or other person, and to consult a lawyer as soon as possible.  
- Keep any documents you receive (e.g., arrest memo, charge sheet) and note the names and badge numbers of the officers involved.  
- You should promptly contact a lawyer or legal‑aid service to discuss the specifics of your case and to protect your rights.  
- Because the exact rules can vary by state and may have been amended, it is important to verify the current law and any recent changes.  

This is general information, not legal advice. Check a primary source or a lawyer before relying on it.
consumer:
- First, gather all documents related to the phone you bought, such as the purchase receipt, warranty card, any correspondence with the seller, and a clear description of the problem you are facing.  
- Write a concise, factual complaint stating the make and model of the phone, the date of purchase, the nature of the defect or issue, and what remedy you are seeking (repair, replacement, refund, etc.).  
- Send this written complaint to the seller or dealer and keep a copy of the sent letter/email as proof of your request.  
- If the seller does not resolve the matter within a reasonable time, you can approach the appropriate consumer dispute body (the consumer commission) that has jurisdiction over your location and the value of the claim.  
- Before filing, you may want to check the consumer helpline or a consumer‑rights website to confirm which level of the consumer commission (district, state or national) is likely to handle your case.  
- You can file the complaint online through the consumer portal or submit a physical application, attaching copies of all supporting documents and a self‑addressed envelope for any notices.  
- The consumer commission will usually issue a notice to the seller, give them an opportunity to respond, and then decide the dispute based on the evidence you both provide.  
- The exact procedure, required forms and any fees can vary depending on the state and the amount involved, so it’s wise to confirm the current rules or get assistance from a consumer‑rights lawyer or legal aid service.  

This is general information, not legal advice. Check a primary source or a lawyer before relying on it.
violence:
- If you are in immediate danger, call the emergency number or the police right away and ask for protection.  
- You can also contact a women’s helpline or a trusted family member or friend for immediate support and shelter.  
- A protection order can be sought to stop the abuse and to keep the abuser away from you and your children; a lawyer or legal‑aid service can help you prepare the necessary written request.  
- Keep any evidence of the abuse (photos, medical reports, messages, witness statements) in a safe place, as it may be needed later.  
- You may approach a legal‑aid organization or a lawyer who can explain the relevant law and guide you on filing a complaint, obtaining a protection order, and any other relief that may be available.  
- The exact steps and the authority that can grant protection depend on the facts, the state you live in, and the current law, which may have been amended.  
- It is important to get professional legal advice as soon as possible to understand all your options and to ensure your safety.  

This is general information, not legal advice. Check a primary source or a lawyer before relying on it.
